items.title: Focus Question: Which principles explain why a hydraulic jack lifts a truck, why a steel ship floats, and why a shower curtain swings inward?

answer.html: Pascal's principle (a pressure change is transmitted undiminished through a confined fluid) explains the jack. Archimedes' principle (buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced) explains the floating ship. Bernoulli's principle (pressure drops where a fluid moves faster) explains the shower curtain.

items.title: Figure 10, Infer: In a hydraulic machine, how would 𝐹2 change if the area 𝐴2 of the output piston were doubled while 𝐹1 and 𝐴1 stayed the same?

body.html: 𝐹<sub>2</sub> = 𝐹<sub>1</sub>𝐴<sub>2</sub> / 𝐴<sub>1</sub>.
The pressure 𝐹<sub>1</sub> / 𝐴<sub>1</sub> is fixed. The output force is that pressure times 𝐴<sub>2</sub>, so 𝐹<sub>2</sub> is directly proportional to 𝐴<sub>2</sub>.

answer.html: 𝐹<sub>2</sub> doubles, because the same pressure now acts on twice the area.

items.title: Practice Problem 24: A barber chair is raised by a hydraulic lift. The chair's piston has an area of 1250 cm² and must supply 2600 N of force. The pump piston has an area of 45 cm². What force must be applied to the pump piston?

body.html: 𝐹<sub>2</sub> = 2600 N, 𝐴<sub>2</sub> = 1250 cm<sup>2</sup>, 𝐴<sub>1</sub> = 45 cm<sup>2</sup>. Find 𝐹<sub>1</sub>.
Pascal's principle: 𝐹<sub>1</sub> / 𝐴<sub>1</sub> = 𝐹<sub>2</sub> / 𝐴<sub>2</sub>. The areas can stay in cm<sup>2</sup> because they appear as a ratio.

check.html: The piston area ratio is about 28, so the force is reduced by about 28 times: 2600 / 28 ≈93.

items.title: Practice Problem 25: A garage jack has an input piston of area 0.012 m² and an output piston of area 1.6 m². A mechanic pushes on the input piston with 85 N. What weight can the jack lift?

body.html: 𝐹<sub>1</sub> = 85 N, 𝐴<sub>1</sub> = 0.012 m<sup>2</sup>, 𝐴<sub>2</sub> = 1.6 m<sup>2</sup>. Find 𝐹<sub>2</sub>.
𝐹<sub>2</sub> = 𝐹<sub>1</sub>𝐴<sub>2</sub> / 𝐴<sub>1</sub>.

check.html: The area ratio is about 133, so 85 × 133 ≈1.1 × 10<sup>4</sup>. That is the weight of a car of about 1,150 kg.

items.title: Practice Problem 26 (Challenge): A small hydraulic press is balanced when a 310-N weight rests on the small piston and a 940-N weight rests on the large piston. What is the ratio of the area of the large piston to the area of the small piston?

body.html: 𝐹<sub>small</sub> = 310 N, 𝐹<sub>large</sub> = 940 N, balanced. Find 𝐴<sub>large</sub> / 𝐴<sub>small</sub>.
Balanced means equal pressure at the two pistons, 𝐹<sub>1</sub> / 𝐴<sub>1</sub> = 𝐹<sub>2</sub> / 𝐴<sub>2</sub>.

answer.html: The large piston has an area 3.0 times the small piston's area (a ratio of 1: 3.0, small to large).

check.html: The heavier load needs the larger piston so that both pressures are equal.

items.title: Figure 13, Describe: Under what condition will an object sink in a fluid?

answer.html: An object sinks when the buoyant force on it is less than its weight, which happens when its average density is greater than the density of the fluid.

items.title: Get It? How does a fish use its swim bladder to rise, sink or stay at one depth?

body.html: Compare the fish's weight with the buoyant force, 𝜌<sub>water</sub>𝑉𝑔. A fish changes its volume (and so its average density) by filling or emptying its gas-filled swim bladder.

If the bladder expands, the fish's volume and the buoyant force increase while its weight stays the same, so it rises. If the bladder shrinks, the buoyant force drops below the weight and the fish sinks. If the two forces are equal, the fish is neutrally buoyant and stays at one depth.

answer.html: Rise: expand the bladder (buoyant force greater than weight). Sink: shrink the bladder (buoyant force less than weight). Stay at one depth: adjust the bladder so that the buoyant force equals the weight (average density equals the water's).

items.title: Get It? Air moves faster over the top of an airplane wing than under it. How does the air pressure on top compare with the pressure underneath?

answer.html: The faster-moving air above the wing has the lower pressure, so the pressure underneath is greater (Bernoulli's principle), which gives an upward net force on the wing.

items.title: Practice Problem 27: A concrete block with a volume of 0.35 m³ and a density 2.4 times that of water is held fully under water. If it is released, what is the net force on it?

body.html: 𝜌<sub>concrete</sub> = 2.4 𝜌<sub>water</sub>, 𝑉= 0.35 m<sup>3</sup>, 𝜌<sub>water</sub> = 1.00 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg/m<sup>3</sup>. Find the net force and its direction.
The net force is the weight minus the buoyant force: 𝐹<sup>net</sup> = 𝐹<sup>𝑔</sup>−𝐹<sup>buoyant</sup> = (𝜌<sub>concrete</sub> −𝜌<sub>water</sub>)𝑉𝑔.

answer.html: 4.8 × 10<sup>3</sup> N downward

check.html: The block is denser than water, so the net force is downward and it sinks. Correct.

items.title: Practice Problem 28: A boy floats at rest in seawater (density 1.03 × 103 kg/m3). His weight is 535 N. What volume of his body is under water?

body.html: Weight 𝐹<sup>𝑔</sup>= 535 N; 𝜌<sub>sea</sub> = 1.03 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg/m<sup>3</sup>. Find the submerged volume.
Floating at rest means the buoyant force equals his weight: 𝜌<sub>sea</sub>𝑉<sup>sub</sup>𝑔= 𝐹<sup>𝑔</sup>.
𝑉<sub>sub</sub> =

check.html: His mass is about 55 kg. Seawater is denser than 1 kg per liter, so about 53 L of it has that mass. It matches.

items.title: Practice Problem 29: A 830-N sensor package is lowered into a lake on a cable. The package has a volume of 9.4 × 10−3 m3. What is the tension in the cable when the package hangs fully submerged and at rest?

body.html: 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub>= 830 N, 𝑉= 9.4 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> m<sup>3</sup>.
The package is in equilibrium: 𝑇+ 𝐹<sup>buoyant</sup> = 𝐹<sup>𝑔</sup>, so 𝑇= 𝐹<sup>𝑔</sup>−𝜌<sub>water</sub>𝑉𝑔.
𝐹<sub>buoyant</sub> = (1.00 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg/m<sup>3</sup>)(9.4 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> m<sup>3</sup>)(9.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>) = 92 N

check.html: The tension is less than the package's weight in air, as it should be.

items.title: Practice Problem 30: A raft is a slab of foam measuring 2.0 m by 1.5 m by 0.10 m. The foam's density is 0.20 times the density of water. How much weight of cargo can be placed on the raft so that it is just fully submerged?

body.html: Foam density = 0.20 𝜌<sub>water</sub>; slab 2.0 m × 1.5 m × 0.10 m, so 𝑉= 0.30 m<sup>3</sup>. Find the weight of cargo for the slab to be just fully submerged.
When the slab is barely submerged, the buoyant force is 𝜌<sub>water</sub>𝑉𝑔, and it must equal the weight of the foam plus the weight of the cargo.

𝐹<sub>buoyant</sub> = (1.00 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg/m<sup>3</sup>)(0.30 m<sup>3</sup>)(9.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>) = 2.9 × 10<sup>3</sup> N 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub><sub>, foam</sub> = (0.20)(1.00 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg/m<sup>3</sup>)(0.30 m<sup>3</sup>)(9.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>) = 5.9 × 10<sup>2</sup> N

body.alt: 𝐹𝑔, cargo = 𝐹buoyant −𝐹𝑔, foam = 2940 N −588 N = 2.4 × 103 N

answer.html: 2.4 × 10<sup>3</sup> N of cargo

check.html: Foam is 20% as dense as water, so 80% of the maximum buoyant force is available for cargo: 0.80 × 2940 ≈2350 N.

items.title: Practice Problem 31 (Challenge): A flat-bottomed boat weighs 650 N. Foam blocks of density 0.12 times that of water are to be packed into it so that it still floats when completely full of water. What minimum volume of foam is needed?

body.html: Boat weight 650 N; foam density 0.12 𝜌<sub>water</sub>. Find the minimum foam volume so that the full-of-water boat still floats.

In the worst case the boat is full of water, so only the foam supplies lift. The buoyant force on the foam must at least equal the weight of the boat plus the foam: 𝜌<sub>water</sub>𝑉𝑔≥𝐹<sup>𝑔</sup><sup>, boat</sup> + 0.12 𝜌<sub>water</sub>𝑉𝑔. (If the foam's own weight is neglected, the volume is slightly smaller.)
Neglecting the foam's weight first: 𝑉<sub>foam</sub> =
Including the foam's weight, each cubic meter gives a net lift of (1 −0.12) 𝜌<sub>water</sub>𝑔: 𝑉<sub>foam</sub> =

answer.html: About 0.07 m<sup>3</sup> (approximately 6.6 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>2</sup> m<sup>3</sup>, or 7.5 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>2</sup> m<sup>3</sup> if the foam's own weight is counted), about 75 L

check.html: This is about 75 L, a few large blocks of foam, which is a reasonable amount for a boat of this size.

items.title: Check Your Progress 32: An egg sinks in a glass of fresh water but floats when a lot of salt is stirred into the water. Explain why, and say what stays the same and what changes.

body.html: The egg displaces the same volume of liquid in both cases and its weight does not change. What changes is the density of the liquid, so the buoyant force 𝜌<sub>liquid</sub>𝑉𝑔 changes.

In fresh water, the buoyant force on the fully submerged egg is less than its weight, so it sinks. Dissolved salt raises the density of the water. When the density of the salt water exceeds the egg's average density, the buoyant force for a fully submerged egg is greater than the egg's weight, so it rises and floats.

answer.html: The salt water is denser than fresh water, so it gives a larger buoyant force on the same volume of egg. The egg's weight is unchanged. In fresh water the egg is denser than the water and sinks; in salt water it is less dense than the water and floats.

items.title: Check Your Progress 33: A stomp launcher for a toy rocket uses a large piston of area 2.8 × 10−3 m2 pushed by your foot with a force of 210 N. It drives air through a tube whose piston area is 3.5 × 10−4 m2. What force acts on the rocket?

body.html: 𝐹<sub>1</sub> = 210 N, 𝐴<sub>1</sub> = 2.8 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> m<sup>2</sup>, 𝐴<sub>2</sub> = 3.5 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>4</sup> m<sup>2</sup>. Find 𝐹<sub>2</sub>.
Pascal's principle, 𝐹<sub>2</sub> = 𝐹<sub>1</sub>𝐴<sub>2</sub> / 𝐴<sub>1</sub>.

check.html: The tube area is smaller, so the force is smaller than the stomp force. The pressure is the same on both: 7.5 × 10<sup>4</sup> Pa.

items.title: Check Your Progress 34: A helium balloon is used to lift a 24-N instrument package. The density of helium is 0.18 kg/m³ and the density of air is 1.2 kg/m³. Find the minimum volume of the balloon, neglecting the weight of the balloon skin.

body.html: Load weight 𝐹<sup>𝑔</sup>= 24 N. 𝜌<sub>He</sub> = 0.18 kg/m<sup>3</sup>, 𝜌<sub>air</sub> = 1.2 kg/m<sup>3</sup> . Find the minimum balloon volume.
The buoyant force (weight of displaced air) must at least equal the weight of the helium plus the load: 𝜌<sub>air</sub>𝑉𝑔= 𝜌<sub>He</sub>𝑉𝑔+ 𝐹<sup>𝑔</sup><sup>, load</sup>.

answer.html: About 2.4 m<sup>3</sup>

check.html: A balloon about 1.7 m across lifts a load of about 2.4 kg. Reasonable.

items.title: Check Your Progress 35: A block of wood floats in fresh water with 35% of its volume below the surface. Find the density of the wood.

body.html: A floating object's weight equals the buoyant force: 𝜌<sub>wood</sub>𝑉𝑔= 𝜌<sub>water</sub>𝑉<sup>sub</sup>𝑔, so 𝜌<sub>wood</sub> = 𝜌<sub>water</sub>(𝑉<sup>sub</sup> / 𝑉).

answer.html: 3.5 × 10<sup>2</sup> kg/m<sup>3</sup> (0.35 g/cm³)

check.html: The wood is less dense than water, which is why it floats, and the value is in the range of light woods such as balsa and cedar.

items.title: Check Your Progress 36: A hydraulic press has an output piston of area 0.11 m² that exerts 1.8 × 104 N, and an input piston of area 0.0064 m². (a) What is the pressure in the fluid? (b) What force acts on the input piston?

body.html: 𝐹<sub>2</sub> = 1.8 × 10<sup>4</sup> N, 𝐴<sub>2</sub> = 0.11 m<sup>2</sup>, 𝐴<sub>1</sub> = 0.0064 m<sup>2</sup>. (a) Find 𝑃. (b) Find 𝐹<sub>1</sub>.
(a) 𝑃= 𝐹/ 𝐴. (b) The same pressure acts on the small piston, so 𝐹<sub>1</sub> = 𝑃𝐴<sub>1</sub>.

check.html: The area ratio is 0.0064 / 0.11 = 0.058, and 1.8 × 10<sup>4</sup> × 0.058 = 1.0 × 10<sup>3</sup>. It matches.

items.title: Check Your Progress 37: Both objects are fully submerged in water. (a) Which displaces more water, a 1.0-kg block of iron or a 1.0-kg block of silver? (b) Which displaces more water, a 25-cm³ block of aluminum or a 25-cm³ block of gold?

body.html: A fully submerged object displaces a volume of water equal to its own volume, 𝑉= 𝑚/ 𝜌. Work (a): Same mass. Iron is less dense (7.87 g/cm<sup>3</sup>) than silver (10.5 g/cm<sup>3</sup>), so the iron block has the larger volume. Work (b): Same volume of 25 cm<sup>3</sup>, so the displaced volumes are equal.

answer.html: (a) The 1.0-kg iron block displaces more water (it has the larger volume). (b) Neither: both 25-cm<sup>3</sup> blocks displace 25 cm<sup>3</sup> of water.

items.title: Check Your Progress 38: Critical thinking. When the shower is running, the shower curtain swings inward toward the water stream. Explain why, using Bernoulli's principle.

body.html: Bernoulli's principle: fast-moving fluid has lower pressure.

The falling water drags the air next to it downward, so the air inside the curtain moves quickly and has lower pressure. The still air outside the curtain stays at the higher room pressure. The pressure difference gives a net inward force on the curtain. To reduce the effect, let air in below the stream or weigh down the hem so that it cannot swing, or open the curtain so that the pressure can equalize.

answer.html: The moving air near the shower stream has lower pressure than the still air outside, so the higher outside pressure pushes the curtain inward.

items.title: Revisit the Encounter the Phenomenon Question: Which Lesson 3 ideas help explain how the liquid moves through the branching channel network?

body.html: Pascal's principle and Bernoulli's principle both apply to fluids in channels.

Pascal's principle: pressure applied to the confined liquid is transmitted through all of its branches. Bernoulli's principle: where a channel narrows, the liquid speeds up and its pressure drops. In very thin channels the flow stays in smooth layers (streamlined flow), so the liquid advances evenly.

answer.html: Pressure is transmitted through the whole liquid, and the flow is faster, with lower pressure, in the narrower branches, provided the flow is smooth rather than turbulent.

items.title: Focus Question: What principles describe the behavior and motion of fluids?

answer.html: Pascal's principle (pressure changes are transmitted undiminished through a confined fluid), Archimedes' principle (buoyant force equals the weight of fluid displaced), and Bernoulli's principle (pressure drops where the fluid speeds up).

items.title: Figure 10, Infer: how would 𝐹2 change if 𝐹1 increased?

body.html: 𝐹<sub>2</sub> = 𝐹<sub>1</sub>𝐴<sub>2</sub> / 𝐴<sub>1</sub>.
𝐴<sub>2</sub> / 𝐴<sub>1</sub> is a fixed constant for the machine, so 𝐹<sub>2</sub> is directly proportional to 𝐹<sub>1</sub>.

answer.html: 𝐹<sub>2</sub> increases in the same proportion as 𝐹<sub>1</sub>, because the extra pressure is transmitted undiminished through the fluid and acts on the fixed area 𝐴<sub>2</sub>.

items.title: Practice Problem 24: Dentist's chair

body.html: 𝐹<sub>2</sub> = 1600 N, 𝐴<sub>2</sub> = 1440 cm<sup>2</sup>, 𝐴<sub>1</sub> = 72 cm<sup>2</sup>. Find 𝐹<sub>1</sub>.
Pascal's principle: 𝐹<sub>1</sub> / 𝐴<sub>1</sub> = 𝐹<sub>2</sub> / 𝐴<sub>2</sub>. The areas can stay in cm<sup>2</sup> because they appear as a ratio.

check.html: The piston area ratio is 20, so the force is reduced by 20 times: 1600 / 20 = 80.

items.title: Practice Problem 25: Mechanic's hydraulic lift

body.html: 𝐹<sub>1</sub> = 55 N, 𝐴<sub>1</sub> = 0.015 m<sup>2</sup>, 𝐴<sub>2</sub> = 2.4 m<sup>2</sup>. Find 𝐹<sub>2</sub> (the car's weight).
𝐹<sub>2</sub> = 𝐹<sub>1</sub>𝐴<sub>2</sub> / 𝐴<sub>1</sub>.

check.html: The area ratio is 160, so 55 × 160 = 8800. A small car weighs about this much.

items.title: Practice Problem 26 (Challenge): Child and adult on pistons

body.html: 𝐹<sub>child</sub> = 400 N, 𝐹<sub>adult</sub> = 1100 N, balanced. Find 𝐴<sub>adult</sub> / 𝐴<sub>child</sub> .
Balanced means equal pressure at the two pistons, 𝐹<sub>1</sub> / 𝐴<sub>1</sub> = 𝐹<sub>2</sub> / 𝐴<sub>2</sub>.

answer.html: The adult's piston has an area 2.75 times the child's piston, so the ratio of areas (child : adult) is 1: 2.75 (about 4 : 11).

check.html: The heavier person needs the larger piston, like a seesaw where the heavier person sits closer to the pivot.

items.title: Figure 13, Describe: when will an object float?

answer.html: An object floats (rises, or stays partly above the surface) when the buoyant force on it is greater than its weight, which happens when its average density is less than the density of the fluid.

items.title: Get It? How can the submersible rise, sink or stay suspended?

body.html: Compare the weight of the submersible with the buoyant force, 𝜌<sub>fluid</sub>𝑉𝑔, which stays fixed for a fixed volume. A submersible changes its weight (average density) by taking in or pumping out water, or by dropping ballast.
If its weight is greater than the buoyant force, it sinks. If its weight is less, it rises. If they are equal, it is neutrally buoyant and stays suspended.

answer.html: Rise: weight less than buoyant force (pump out water or drop ballast). Sink: weight greater than buoyant force (take in water). Suspended: weight equals buoyant force (average density equals the water's density).

items.title: Get It? Relationship between fluid velocity and pressure (Bernoulli)

answer.html: As the speed of a fluid increases, the pressure it exerts decreases (and where the speed is lower, the pressure is greater).

items.title: Practice Problem 27: Net force on a brick block under water

body.html: 𝜌<sub>brick</sub> = 1.8 𝜌<sub>water</sub>, 𝑉= 0.20 m<sup>3</sup>, 𝜌<sub>water</sub> = 1.00 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg/m<sup>3</sup>.
The net force is the weight minus the buoyant force: 𝐹<sup>net</sup> = 𝐹<sup>𝑔</sup>−𝐹<sup>buoyant</sup> = (𝜌<sub>brick</sub> −𝜌<sub>water</sub>)𝑉𝑔.

answer.html: 1.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> N downward

check.html: The block sinks, since it is denser than water, as expected for a downward net force.

items.title: Practice Problem 28: Girl floating in a lake

body.html: Weight 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub>= 610 N; fresh water 1.00 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg/m<sup>3</sup>. Find the submerged volume.
Floating at rest means the buoyant force equals her weight: 𝜌<sub>water</sub>𝑉<sup>sub</sup>𝑔= 𝐹<sup>𝑔</sup>.
𝑉<sub>sub</sub> =

answer.html: 6.2 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>2</sup> m<sup>3</sup> (62 L)

check.html: Her mass is about 62 kg, so a volume of 62 L (nearly the density of water) makes sense.

items.title: Practice Problem 29: Tension in the wire supporting a submerged camera

body.html: 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub>= 1250 N, 𝑉= 16.5 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> m<sup>3</sup>.
The camera is in equilibrium: 𝑇+ 𝐹<sup>buoyant</sup> = 𝐹<sup>𝑔</sup>, so 𝑇= 𝐹<sup>𝑔</sup>−𝜌<sub>water</sub>𝑉𝑔.
𝐹<sub>buoyant</sub> = (1.00 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg/m<sup>3</sup>)(16.5 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> m<sup>3</sup>)(9.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>) = 162 N

items.title: Practice Problem 30: Bricks on a foam slab

body.html: Foam density = 0.10 𝜌<sub>water</sub>; slab 1.0 m × 1.0 m × 0.10 m, so 𝑉= 0.10 m<sup>3</sup>. Find the weight of bricks so that the slab is just fully submerged.
When the slab is barely submerged, the buoyant force is 𝜌<sub>water</sub>𝑉𝑔 and it must equal the weight of the foam plus the weight of the bricks.

𝐹<sub>buoyant</sub> = (1.00 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg/m<sup>3</sup>)(0.10 m<sup>3</sup>)(9.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>) = 9.8 × 10<sup>2</sup> N 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub><sub>, foam</sub> = (0.10)(1.00 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg/m<sup>3</sup>)(0.10 m<sup>3</sup>)(9.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>) = 98 N

answer.html: 8.8 × 10<sup>2</sup> N of bricks

check.html: Foam is 10% as dense as water, so 90% of the maximum buoyant force is available to carry cargo: 0.9 × 980 ≈880 N.

items.title: Practice Problem 31 (Challenge): Foam for a canoe

body.html: Canoe weight 480 N. Find the minimum foam volume so that the filled canoe still floats.

Take the worst case of a canoe full of water, so the foam must supply a buoyant force at least equal to the canoe's weight: 𝜌<sub>water</sub>𝑉<sup>foam</sup>𝑔≥𝐹<sup>𝑔</sup><sup>, canoe</sup>. (Using the foam density from Problem 30, the foam's own weight, 0.10 𝜌<sub>water</sub>𝑉𝑔, is small, so including it would raise the answer only slightly.)
𝑉<sub>foam</sub> =
If the foam's own weight is included, the net lift per unit volume is 0.90 𝜌<sub>water</sub>𝑔 and the volume becomes 5.4 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>2</sup> m<sup>3</sup>.

answer.html: About 0.05 m<sup>3</sup> (approximately 4.9 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>2</sup> m<sup>3</sup>, or 5.4 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>2</sup> m<sup>3</sup> if the foam's own weight is counted), about 50 L

check.html: This is about 50 L, the size of a few large blocks of foam, a reasonable amount.

items.title: Check Your Progress 32: Soda cans that sink and float

body.html: The cans displace equal volumes of water, so the buoyant forces are equal. The can that floats must have a smaller weight (lower average density).

A can of regular soda contains a lot of dissolved sugar, which makes its average density greater than water's, so it sinks. A diet can contains only a tiny mass of artificial sweetener, so its average density is below water's, and it floats.

answer.html: The difference is mass (average density). The can that floats has a smaller mass (less dissolved sugar, as in diet soda) so its weight is less than the buoyant force.

items.title: Check Your Progress 33: Toy rocket launcher

body.html: 𝐹<sub>1</sub> = 150 N, 𝐴<sub>1</sub> = 2.5 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> m<sup>2</sup>, 𝐴<sub>2</sub> = 4.0 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>4</sup> m<sup>2</sup>. Find 𝐹<sub>2</sub>.
Pascal's principle, 𝐹<sub>2</sub> = 𝐹<sub>1</sub>𝐴<sub>2</sub> / 𝐴<sub>1</sub>.

check.html: The launch tube area is smaller, so the force is smaller than the stomp force. The pressure is the same: 6.0 × 10<sup>4</sup> Pa.

items.title: Check Your Progress 34: Helium balloon lifting the brick

items.title: Check Your Progress 37: Which displaces more water?

body.html: A fully submerged object displaces a volume of water equal to its own volume, 𝑉= 𝑚/ 𝜌. Work (a): Same mass of 1.0 kg. Aluminum is less dense (2.7 g/cm<sup>3</sup>) than lead (11.3 g/cm<sup>3</sup>), so its volume is greater. Work (b): Same volume of 10 cm<sup>3</sup>, so the displaced volumes are equal.

answer.html: (a) The 1.0-kg aluminum block displaces more water (it has the larger volume). (b) Neither: both 10-cm<sup>3</sup> blocks displace the same 10 cm<sup>3</sup> of water.

items.title: Check Your Progress 38: Critical thinking, tornado and the exploding house

body.html: Bernoulli's principle: fast-moving air has low pressure.

The tornado's winds near the house are very fast, so the outside pressure is much lower than the pressure of the still air inside. The pressure difference gives a net outward force on walls, windows and the roof, which can push them out (an "explosion"). To reduce the danger, equalize the pressure by providing vents so that inside and outside pressures are similar quickly. Windows opened slightly on the side away from the storm are the textbook remedy, although in practice, the best protection is a reinforced structure and a storm shelter.

answer.html: The tornado's fast air has low pressure, so the higher inside pressure pushes outward on doors and windows. Allowing air to escape or flow through (opened vents or windows) equalizes the pressure and reduces the net outward force.

items.title: Revisit the Encounter the Phenomenon Question

body.html: Which Lesson 3 ideas help explain the fluid in the branching device?

Pascal's principle: pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted through all of its branches. Bernoulli's principle: where the channel narrows the fluid speeds up and its pressure drops. Streamlined (not turbulent) flow in thin channels stays in smooth layers, so the liquid advances evenly through the grooves.

answer.html: Pressure is transmitted undiminished throughout the fluid, and the flow speeds up (with lower pressure) in narrower branches, as long as the flow is smooth (streamlined) rather than turbulent.
